decision.canApiDoIt: No. The Strava API physically cannot create a route, and no scope, access tier or subscription changes that. Strava's own machine-readable spec (developers.strava.com/swagger/swagger.json) contains 31 operations; exactly two of them are POSTs — POST /activities and POST /uploads — and both create ACTIVITIES (a recorded run). Routes appear only as five read-only GETs. There is no POST /routes, and no write scope that could authorise one exists (the full scope list is read, read_all, profile:read_all, profile:write, activity:read, activity:read_all, activity:write). The Strava MCP server connected to your Claude account is also read-only — it has no write tool of any kind. Anyone claiming a Strava route-creation endpoint is describing Strava's internal website API, which is cookie/CSRF-authenticated, undocumented, and outside the terms attached to client id 262848 (the one shared with DoHardThings). So: the token you already have cannot do this, and neither could a fresh one.

research.verdict: There is NO endpoint in the public Strava API that creates a route. This is not an inference from silence — I enumerated every path and method in Strava's own OpenAPI spec (developers.strava.com/swagger/swagger.json). The spec contains exactly two POST paths (/activities, /uploads) and three PUT paths (/athlete, /activities/{id}, /segments/{id}/starred). Routes appear only as four GET paths plus a streams GET. Nothing writes a route. Correspondingly, there is no route:write or routes:write scope — the complete scope list is read, read_all, profile:read_all, profile:write, activity:read, activity:read_all, activity:write, and the only write scopes cover profile fields, segment starring, and activities/uploads. POST /uploads is documented as "Upload Activity"; its parameters are file, data_type, sport_type, name, description, trainer, commute, external_id, and its data_type values are fit, fit.gz, tcx, tcx.gz, gpx, gpx.gz, json. None of those parameters selects "route" — there is no flag, no alternate data_type, nothing. Sending the routr GPX to POST /uploads WILL create an activity (a recorded run Luis did not do), which is precisely the outcome to avoid. So: the GPX cannot be turned into a Strava route by any documented API call, with any scope, at any access tier. Anything that appears to do this is either Strava's own logged-in website using private internal endpoints, or a third-party tool driving that website.

I confirmed this two independent ways: (a) the current support article "Uploading Route Files" describes it verbatim; (b) the live route-builder page at strava.com/maps/create ships a UI string table containing "Upload GPX" / "Import GPX" / "Choose File" plus GPX-specific error messages, so the control is present in production today. Two important caveats. First, route creation is a Strava-subscription feature — Strava's own "What Features Are Included in a Strava Subscription" article lists "Create Routes: Create routes from scratch on the Strava website and the Strava mobile app" under paid features, so if Luis is on a free account the save may be blocked or degraded (see caveats — the live bundle's gating is an upsell rather than an obvious hard wall, and I could not verify his account state without calling Strava). Second, the URL has moved: strava.com/routes/new now 301-redirects to strava.com/maps/create. There is NO documented public-API equivalent surfaced anywhere in Strava's help centre — the website is the path. Mobile app: route creation exists on mobile (Maps tab > Create Route) but the documented mobile builder is tap/draw/sketch only — no GPX file import on mobile. The GPX import is desktop-web only, and the builder even shows a "Made for your desktop" modal on small screens.

2. In the route builder, click the "Upload GPX" button in the floating route toolbar on the map (the same toolbar holds Reverse Route / Undo / Redo / Clear / Save Route).
3. In the "Import GPX" modal, click "Choose File" and pick the file — /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-luisdeburnay-dev-routr/0f6602a3-b43a-46c6-b392-056cf6dbcf31/scratchpad/route.gpx
4. If Strava says "This GPX file does not contain a sport type", pick one from the "Route Type" dropdown in the same modal — choose Run. (The routr-generated GPX almost certainly has no sport type, so expect this prompt.) Then confirm with "Import GPX".
5. The track loads as an editable route. Optionally adjust waypoints or routing preferences. Then click "Save Route".
6. In the save dialog: enter a "Route name (required)", set visibility ("Everyone" or "Only You" — "Only You" is fine and still syncs to a watch), and toggle "Star Route" ON. The dialog's own footnote for that toggle reads "Send your Route to your device (requires a compatible device)" — this star is what triggers the Garmin sync.
7. Click "Save to My Routes".

THEN, TO GET IT ONTO THE FENIX 8:
8. One-time only: in Garmin Connect, enable the Courses permission for Strava. Web: https://connect.garmin.com/modern/settings/accountInformation. Mobile: Garmin Connect app > "More" tab > Settings > Connected Apps > Strava > enable Courses permission.
9. The route must be starred/saved (step 6). If it was already starred, un-star it and re-star it — Strava's docs are explicit that re-starring is what re-triggers a sync.
10. Sync the watch with the Garmin Connect mobile app (Bluetooth/Wi-Fi) or Garmin Express. The route appears in the Courses folder on the Fenix 8. Route must be under 600 miles.

MOBILE APP (for completeness — cannot do GPX import): Maps tab > "Create Route" (bottom right) > tap points or use the pencil to sketch > Save. Tap/draw only; there is no file picker.

NOTE ON A NON-STRAVA SHORTCUT: since the goal is navigation on a Fenix 8, the GPX can also be dropped straight into Garmin Connect as a Course (Garmin Connect > Training & Planning > Courses > Import), bypassing Strava entirely and bypassing any Strava subscription question. Out of scope for this angle but worth flagging to whoever acts on this.
research.subscriptionRequired:
Almost certainly YES for saving the route, and this is the single biggest risk to the plan. Strava's current article "What Features Are Included in a Strava Subscription" lists under "Route Exploration": "Create Routes: Create routes from scratch on the Strava website and the Strava mobile app." Both route-builder articles open with the same gate — "Routes on Web": "With a Strava subscription, you can create new routes from scratch by clicking the 'Create Route' button near the top of the My Routes page." "Creating Routes on Mobile": "With a Strava subscription, you can build new routes from scratch on the Strava mobile app."

What a FREE account definitely still gets: recording and uploading activities (Strava's "Is Strava Free" article: "Yes, Strava is a free app, and there is no cost to record and share your activities"); starring other athletes' public routes; viewing and following routes; exporting any public route as GPX or TCX; syncing starred routes to a Garmin.

The honest uncertainty: the "Uploading Route Files" article itself does NOT mention a subscription, and the live builder bundle's paywall for this area is a soft "Customize this route — Get all our route planning tools with a Strava subscription" upsell attached to the SAVE modal (with "Not right now" / "Subscribe" buttons) rather than an obvious hard block on the builder. That leaves open the possibility that a free user can import and save a GPX-derived route while being denied the planning preferences (elevation/surface/popularity bias). I could not resolve this without touching Luis's account, which the brief forbids. Whoever acts on this should check his subscription state first — either by looking at his Strava profile for the subscriber badge, or by calling the Strava MCP server's read-only `eligibility` tool, which I deliberately did not call.

missed: GEOMETRY FIDELITY IS UNVERIFIED AND IT MATTERS MOST HERE. The whole point of a routr GPX is its surface-classified line choice. Strava's own article says that after import you 'adjust the waypoints or route preferences' — which implies the imported track becomes an editable route object, and route objects on Strava are normally snapped to Strava's own routable network. I grepped the live bundle for any snap/follow-roads/preserve-original toggle and found none, so there is no visible user control over this. Cheapest check: after saving, export the route back out and diff it against the source GPX.

THE EXPORT-BACK VERIFICATION LOOP EXISTS AND WAS NOT MENTIONED. GET /routes/{id}/export_gpx and GET /athletes/{id}/routes are both in the current official spec, so once the route is created by hand it CAN be pulled back programmatically to confirm what Strava actually stored. That is the mechanism for the fidelity check above.

SCOPE TRAP ON THAT VERIFICATION LOOP. The spec states plainly: '/routes/{id}/export_gpx ... Requires read_all scope for private routes' and '/athletes/{id}/routes ... Private routes are filtered out unless requested by a token with read_all scope.' Luis's stored token has read, activity:write, activity:read_all — it does NOT have read_all. So if he saves the route as 'Only You' (which the other agent recommended), the existing token cannot see or export it at all; it would need a re-auth adding read_all. Save as 'Everyone', or re-auth, or skip the check. The findings' scope column said 'none — browser session', which is right for the click-path but silently misses this downstream consequence.

THE SUBSCRIPTION QUESTION IS CHEAPLY RESOLVABLE READ-ONLY AND SHOULD BE THE FIRST ACTION. The connected Strava MCP server exposes get_athlete_profile and eligibility, both read-only. The other agent deliberately did not call them, which respected the brief, but whoever acts next should call one FIRST — it costs one call and settles the single biggest risk before Luis is sent down a seven-step click path that may dead-end at a paywall.

MINOR: the Garmin Connect direct-Course-import alternative the findings flagged as an aside deserves promotion, precisely because of the two risks above. Importing the GPX straight into Garmin Connect > Courses sidesteps the subscription question entirely AND avoids any Strava re-snapping of the geometry. If the actual goal is 'this exact line, navigable on the Fenix 8', that path is strictly safer; Strava is the right path only if Luis also wants the route living in his Strava My Routes.

research.verdict: Skip Strava entirely for this goal. The shortest path to a navigable 6.06 km course on the Fenix 8 is Garmin Connect's own GPX-to-course import — roughly four clicks in a browser, free, no subscription, and the course reaches the watch over Garmin's normal sync. If it needs to be automated, the same thing is a documented-by-reverse-engineering two-call internal API (POST /course-service/course/import to parse the GPX, POST /course-service/course to save it), plus an optional third call to force it onto the watch immediately. Two hard corrections to the brief's premises: (1) python-garminconnect has ZERO course support — I grepped the installed 0.3.11 source (3743 lines) and there is no upload_course, no get_courses, no /course-service string anywhere; you would use its generic self.client.post("connectapi", path, json=...) escape hatch, which is exactly how its own push_workout_to_device is built. (2) There is NO working authenticated Garmin session on this machine — no ~/.garminconnect, no ~/.garth, no token JSON anywhere under $HOME, and rocket's own docs/specs/07-wiring-todo.md still lists "[ ] Garmin: one-time interactive auth (MFA) on the server" as unticked. The only Garmin artefact present is a GDPR data-export zip at /Users/luisdeburnay/garmin-export/2026-09-08/. So the "automated" path costs an interactive MFA login first, which is most of the effort the manual path would have cost anyway. Hence: for a single 6 km route, do it in the browser. The other services (RideWithGPS, Komoot, plotaroute) all add an account and a sync hop to reach the same Garmin Connect course, so they are strictly worse here. USB/MTP sideloading is the worst option on macOS — the Fenix 8 speaks MTP, which Finder cannot mount, and GARMIN/Courses wants a FIT course file, not the GPX you have.

endpoints.path: https://connect.garmin.com/course-service/course/import (older code uses the /modern/proxy/ or /gc-api/ prefix; the bare path is what garminconnect's connectapi helper takes)
endpoints.creates: neither — it is a parse-only step. It accepts a multipart upload (field name "file", tuple (filename, bytes, "application/octet-stream"), header nk: NT) and returns a course skeleton containing a geoPoints array of {latitude, longitude, elevation}. It does NOT persist anything; RouteTimer's spike notes it returns geoPoints "but no distance, bounding box, or start point".
endpoints.scopesRequired: None in the OAuth sense — this is not the Garmin developer API. It rides a logged-in Garmin Connect web session (Bearer token from python-garminconnect's mobile SSO flow, or a browser SESSION cookie). Garmin's official Connect Developer Program is a separate thing and, per rocket's own integration spec, "rejects personal-use applications".
endpoints.note: Confirmed in 8+ independent OSS implementations across Python, Go, C#, JS. Step 1 of 2.

endpoints.creates: route — this is the Garmin analogue of a Strava Route. Returns the saved course with a courseId, visible at https://connect.garmin.com/modern/course/<courseId>.
endpoints.scopesRequired: Same logged-in Garmin Connect session as above.
endpoints.note: JSON body. Keys seen consistently across implementations: courseName, description, activityTypePk (1 = running), distanceMeter, elevationGainMeter, elevationLossMeter, geoPoints, coursePoints, startPoint, boundingBox {lowerLeft, upperRight}, courseLines, sourceTypeId: 3 (meaning GPX-sourced), rulePK: 2 (private). The caller must compute distance (haversine over geoPoints) and the bounding box itself — the import step does not supply them. That arithmetic is the only real work in the whole automated path.

endpoints.creates: neither — queues an already-saved course for delivery to a specific watch.
endpoints.note: Body MUST be a JSON array, not a bare object — repwise's notes record that a bare object returns HTTP 500 and PUT returns 405. Course payload: [{"deviceId": <userDeviceId>, "messageUrl": "course-service/course/fit/<courseId>", "messageType": "courses", "messageName": "<course name>", "groupName": null, "priority": 1, "fileType": "FIT", "metaDataId": <courseId>}]. Yeetii/strava's variant appends /<deviceId>?elevation=true to messageUrl. deviceId is required — there is no broadcast form; get it from garminconnect's get_device_last_used()["userDeviceId"]. This is OPTIONAL: courses normally sync to the watch on their own via the Garmin Connect phone app. It only buys you immediacy.

endpoints.creates: neither — downloads the course as a FIT course file.
endpoints.note: Relevant only to the USB path: this is where you would get a real FIT course file to drop into GARMIN/Courses. Note the chicken-and-egg — you need the course to exist in Garmin Connect first, at which point USB is pointless. A GPX sibling exists at /course-service/course/gpx/<courseId>.

endpoints.creates: activity — NOT a route. This is the trap.
endpoints.note: Called out explicitly as the thing to avoid. python-garminconnect's ActivityUploadFormat enum accepts FIT, GPX and TCX, so upload_activity("route.gpx") will happily succeed — and log a run Luis has not done, on Garmin, which then re-exports to Strava. Same wrong outcome as the Strava /uploads endpoint, one system upstream. There is also upload_activity_import() which the library documents as "not re-exported to third parties like Strava", but it still creates an activity, so it is still wrong.

endpoints.scopesRequired: "An API client is required for all API requests" — you register a client against your account. The docs page did not state whether approval is automatic or gated; it points questions at developers@ridewithgps.com.
endpoints.note: A real, publicly documented API with a Routes resource — the only alternative service here with genuinely open docs. But I could NOT confirm from the docs page that it accepts a GPX upload to create a route, and it still leaves you needing a RideWithGPS-to-Garmin sync hop.
